Entry
EN-try
n.
From Old French entree, from Latin intrare, to go in. Webster 1828: the passage by which persons enter a house; the act of entering. In the prophets the entry of a gate is where the decisive thing stands — an image of jealousy, or a call to wisdom.

Biblical Definition

Ezekiel, carried in vision to Jerusalem, is told to look and is shown what stands at the way in: behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry (Ezekiel 8:5). The idol is not hidden in a back chamber; it is at the entry, the first thing met, and the chapter goes on to greater abominations within. Where a thing is placed is part of what it means. Wisdom, by contrast, takes her stand at the same kind of place and calls aloud: She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors (Proverbs 8:3) — not in the schools but at the traffic, where ordinary people pass. Jeremiah is sent to a specific gate to break a bottle and pronounce a judgment: go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the east gate (Jeremiah 19:2). And Kings records a king dismantling the temple approaches to please a foreign power: the king's entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD for the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ENTRY as the passage by which persons enter a house or other building; the act of entering; ingress; also the act of recording or setting down in writing.

ENTRY, n. — The passage by which persons enter a house or other building.

The act of entering; ingress; as the entry of a person into a house.

The act of taking possession of lands or tenements.

The act of committing to writing, or of recording in a book.

Old French entree, from Latin intrare, to enter, from intra, within.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 8:5 — "Then said he unto me, Son of man, lift up thine eyes now the way toward the north. So I lifted up mine eyes the way toward the north, and behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry."

Proverbs 8:3 — "She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors."

Jeremiah 19:2 — "And go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the east gate, and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee,"

2 Kings 16:18 — "And the covert for the sabbath that they had built in the house, and the king's entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD for the king of Assyria."

Modern Corruption

2 Kings 16:18 records a king altering the house of the LORD to accommodate a foreign power, and the alteration was architectural before it was theological.

expand to see more

Ahaz had already sent the silver and gold of the temple to Tiglath-pileser and had copied a Damascus altar for the temple court; here he removes the sabbath covert and the king’s outer entry for the king of Assyria. Nothing in the verse is presented as doctrinal reform. It is a rearrangement of approaches to suit an audience whose approval was needed, and the theology followed the furniture. The pattern is worth naming because it is the ordinary sequence of compromise in a church: the arrangement of the service, the placement of the pulpit and the table, what is said at the door and what is left unsaid, all adjusted for the sake of a hearer whose favour is wanted — and doctrine settles afterward into the shape of the room. The regulative principle of worship exists to prevent exactly this drift.

Proverbs 8:3 sets wisdom where the traffic is. She does not wait to be sought in a lecture hall; she cries at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors, where the commerce and the courts and the ordinary business of the town went on. This bears on how the church conceives of its teaching. The wisdom literature assumes an audience of tradesmen, farmers, wives and young men, and addresses them where they are without lowering what it says. That is a different thing from the modern instinct to simplify by subtraction. Wisdom stands in the gate and speaks of righteousness, of the fear of the LORD, and of her own presence at the creation — the highest matter in the book — to whoever is passing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mabo (H3996), an entrance or coming in; pethach (H6607), an opening or doorway; shaar (H8179), a gate; Greek eisodos (G1529), an entrance.

expand to see more

Hebrew mabo (H3996) — an entrance, a coming in; at the entry of the city (Proverbs 8:3) and the king’s entry (2 Kings 16:18).

Hebrew pethach (H6607) — an opening or doorway; this image of jealousy in the entry (Ezekiel 8:5).

Hebrew shaar (H8179) — a gate, the place of counsel, court and commerce in an Israelite city.

Hebrew qinah (H7068) — jealousy or zeal; the name given to the idol at the entry (Ezekiel 8:5).

Greek eisodos (G1529) — an entrance or way in; the New Testament counterpart term.

Usage

"This image of jealousy in the entry (Ezekiel 8:5) — not hidden in a back chamber but at the way in."

"She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city (Proverbs 8:3) — wisdom standing where the traffic is."

"The king's entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD for the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:18) — the furniture moved first."
